parts.latex:
Team $A$ and Team $B$ have entered a chess competition.

Team $A$ and Team $B$ have three members each. Each member of Team $A$ must play each member of Team $B$ once.

Which of the following network diagrams could represent the chess games to be played?

solutions.latex:
Each of the 3 members of Team $A$ plays each of the 3 members of Team $B$ once, so there are $3\times 3 = 9$ games, and so 9 edges.

No one plays a team-mate, so every edge joins a member of $A$ to a member of $B$.

Count the edges in each diagram:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{A} &: 6 \text{ edges} \\ \text{B} &: 6 + 3 = 9 \text{ edges} \\ \text{C} &: 12 \text{ edges} \\ \text{D} &: 15 \text{ edges} \end{aligned}$$
Only diagram B has 9 edges.

In B, label the vertices $1$ to $6$ around the hexagon, and let Team $A$ be the odd vertices and Team $B$ the even vertices. The hexagon sides and the three long diagonals each join an odd vertex to an even vertex, and each odd vertex is joined to all three even vertices.
$$\therefore\ \text{Diagram B}$$

parts.latex: The network diagrams show the 4 roates that a garbage truck travels in one week. Which diagram will allow the truck driver to travel each road exactly once?

solutions.latex:
A route can be travelled using every road exactly once when the network has at most two vertices of odd degree (an Euler path).

Count the degree of each vertex in each diagram.

Diagram A:
$$\begin{aligned} A&=2, \ B=4, \ C=4, \ D=3 \\ E&=4, \ F=5, \ G=2, \ H=2 \end{aligned}$$
Only $D$ and $F$ are odd, so an Euler path exists (from $D$ to $F$).

Diagram B has four odd vertices: $B, D, F, G$.

Diagram C has four odd vertices: $A, C, F, G$.

Diagram D has four odd vertices: $A, E, F, J$.

So only diagram A allows every road to be travelled exactly once.
$$\therefore\ \text{option A}$$

solutions.latex:

The degree of a vertex is the number of edges meeting at it.

C: the path $KMNO$ does not return to $K$, so it is not a cycle.

Hence the answer is option A.

parts.latex:
Two teams have entered a singles tennis team competition. There are three members in each team. Every member of each team must play each of the other team’s members once.

Which of the following network diagrams could represent the tennis to be played?

solutions.latex:
Each of the 3 players in one team plays each of the 3 players in the other team once.

So the network has 6 vertices, and every vertex is joined to exactly the 3 players of the other team.

Number of matches:
$$3\times 3 = 9 \text{ edges}$$
No two players in the same team are joined, and each vertex has degree 3.

Option D has 9 edges: the 6 sides of the hexagon and 3 diagonals through the centre. Each vertex has degree 3. Alternate vertices of the hexagon form the two teams, since the sides join opposite teams and each diagonal joins opposite vertices (one from each team).

The others fail:

A: the vertices have degree 4, so there are more than 9 edges.

B: every pair of vertices is joined (15 edges), which would include players from the same team.

C: only 6 edges.

Hence the answer is option D.

meta.self_check: Model is K(3,3): 9 edges, all degrees 3; option D is a hexagon with 3 long diagonals, which is K(3,3).

parts.latex:
In a club meeting, 5 regular members and the club president are in attendance.

The club rules state that each regular member must shake the hand of \textbf{two} other regular members, and the club president must shake everyone’s hand.

Which network diagram can be used to represent the handshakes between group members?

solutions.latex:
Represent people as vertices and handshakes as edges.

Each of the 5 regular members shakes hands with exactly two other regular members, so the regular members form a single loop of 5 (each has 2 edges among themselves).

The president shakes hands with all 5 members, so the president's vertex is joined to every other vertex (degree 5).

Then each regular member has degree $2+1=3$, and there is one handshake per pair (no repeated edges).

Option A has an outer loop through the 5 regular members, with the centre vertex joined to all 5. Each outer vertex has degree 3 and the centre has degree 5.

Option B has regular members of degree 1, option C has repeated edges (double handshakes), and in option D the regular members have too many handshakes.

$$\therefore\ \text{the diagram is option A.}$$

solutions.latex:
The sum of the degrees of all vertices equals twice the number of edges, since each edge adds 1 to the degree of each of its two ends.

Counting the degrees from the network:
$$\begin{aligned} \deg A &= 3 \ (AC, AB, \text{curved } AB) \\ \deg B &= 5 \ (AB, \text{curved } AB, CB, DB, EB) \\ \deg C &= 3 \ (CA, CD, CB) \\ \deg D &= 3 \ (DC, DB, DE) \\ \deg E &= 2 \ (ED, EB) \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Sum} &= 3+5+3+3+2 \\ &= 16 \end{aligned}$$

Check: there are 8 edges, and $2\times 8 = 16$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the sum of the degrees is } 16 \text{ (option C)}$$

Count the vertices, edges and the degree (number of edges meeting) of each vertex.

parts.latex:
The sum of the degrees of all the vertices in the graph below is:

\exfigure{3305_q1_1}

solutions.latex:
The sum of the degrees of all the vertices equals the sum of the number of edges meeting at each vertex. Count the edges at each vertex.
$$\begin{aligned} \deg A &= 2 &&(AB,\ AE)\\ \deg B &= 3 &&(AB,\ BC,\ BD)\\ \deg C &= 3 &&(BC,\ CD,\ CE)\\ \deg D &= 3 &&(BD,\ CD,\ DE)\\ \deg E &= 3 &&(AE,\ CE,\ DE) \end{aligned}$$
The numbers on the edges are weights (distances), not degrees, so they are not added.
$$2+3+3+3+3 = 14$$
Check: there are $7$ edges, and each edge adds $2$ to the sum of the degrees, so the sum is $2\times 7 = 14$.

Therefore the sum of the degrees is $14$, which is option B.
